description: Hey! We are a team of software developers passionate about code, and we aim to take our expertise to the international stage to help as many people as possible.
summary:
Voraxis is a working observatory that turns two NISAR radar passes over the same area into traceable information about what changed on the ground. We built the whole pipeline: resumable downloads of GCOV scenes, conversion to COGs, a log-ratio difference with an adaptive threshold, segmentation and vectorisation, per-polygon metrics, and publication as vector tiles and GeoJSON. Each detected change is linked to context for the interval — USGS earthquakes, NASA FIRMS fire detections and NASA POWER rainfall — and turned into a tentative hypothesis (POSSIBLE_FLOODING, POSSIBLE_BURN_SCAR and so on) with a confidence level, the reasons behind it and explicit limitations. The interface shows the same screens at two levels: plain-language exploration and a scientific view with decibels, thresholds and raw codes.
It addresses the challenge of making SAR usable. Radar sees through clouds and at night, but raw backscatter is unreadable to decision-makers and easy to overstate. On a real Petén, Guatemala pair spanning 12 days, we detected 6,670 changes over 837 km², with 99.6% valid pixels and 61 fire detections in the context. Nothing in the product claims more than the data supports: change_score is not a probability, and matching in space and time is not causation. That restraint, plus downloadable evidence, is what makes the result usable for monitoring and for accountable decisions.
details:
What it does and how it works. Voraxis compares two NISAR radar passes over the same area and reports what changed, with evidence. The backend downloads the GCOV products (resumable, range-based, several GB each), converts them to Cloud-Optimised GeoTIFFs, computes a log-ratio difference with an adaptive threshold derived from each scene, segments and vectorises the changed areas, and stores one polygon per contiguous change with its metrics in PostGIS. Each polygon is then compared against context for the exact interval: USGS earthquakes, NASA FIRMS active-fire detections and NASA POWER rainfall cells, scored by distance and lead time. A rule engine proposes a tentative type — POSSIBLE_FLOODING, POSSIBLE_BURN_SCAR, POSSIBLE_FLOODED_VEGETATION and so on — with a confidence level, the reasons behind it and the limitations that apply. Results are served as vector tiles, GeoJSON, difference rasters and downloads.

Benefits. Clouds and darkness do not block radar, so the method works in places where optical imagery fails. Every statement in the interface links back to a measured value: decibels, thresholds, valid-pixel percentage, the fires or rain that were actually recorded. Users can explore in plain language or switch to a scientific view with raw codes and processing metadata, and they can filter changes by area, type, date and score, then export the layers.

Intended impact. Faster, more accountable triage of flood, fire and land-change events in tropical and frequently clouded regions. On a real Petén, Guatemala pair spanning 12 days we detected 6,670 changes over 837 km² with 99.6% valid pixels and 61 fire detections nearby. The point is not to declare a disaster from orbit, but to hand an analyst a defensible starting point.

Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, TanStack Query and Zustand on the front end; Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and Alembic with PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Redis and RQ workers, MinIO object storage, rasterio and GDAL on the back end; Docker Compose to run it; pytest for 117 backend tests plus 84 checks against the live API. Data comes from ASF DAAC, USGS, NASA FIRMS, NASA POWER and OpenStreetMap. No special hardware: commodity CPU, no GPU.

Creativity. The design treats uncertainty as a feature: classifications are named hypotheses, change_score is explicitly not a probability, and coincidence is never presented as cause. Pairing that rigour with an editorial visual identity, plus a two-mode interface over the same screens, is what makes the tool readable by non-specialists without hiding the science.

What we considered. Comparable product type, maturity and polarisation between dates; software-version offsets between scenes; noise floor, swath edges and minimum area; graceful degradation when a catalogue is unavailable or unconfigured; bilingual Spanish/English copy; accessibility and honest sourcing of every figure.
